title: Justice augmentation: Activity exceeds proven access gains
desc: Frames AI as capacity expansion for unmet need, balancing urgency against task-specific evidence and preservation of human relationships.

kps.k: The cluster frames AI as a way to expand help for unmet civil legal need, not merely to reduce lawyers’ costs.
kps.d: The central proposition is that AI could increase legal-aid capacity and make legal information easier to obtain for people facing eviction, benefit denials and other urgent problems. Speakers invoke large justice-gap estimates, but these describe different populations and measures: Cat Moon cites 80–90% of legal problems receiving no expert attention, subject to study and jurisdiction; Ashley Oborn invokes a 92% gap; LawNext states that over 90% of US civil legal needs go unrepresented. The excerpts do not establish comparable denominators or methodologies. Colleen Chien explicitly treats AI’s equalising potential as a goal requiring deliberate investigation, rather than an automatic consequence of adoption.

qs.q: And when we talk about access to justice, in the US at least, we can talk about it on a number of levels, but I think that fundamentally, we just have a lot of people, millions of people, really across economic spectrums, who simply do not get any meaningful help with their legal problems, depending on what study you look at, what jurisdiction you're in.
qs.a: AI's Potential for Access to Justice · Access to justice · 2023

qs.q: It can be upwards of 80 to 90 percent of legal problems are not attended to by any kind of legal expert.
qs.a: AI's Potential for Access to Justice · Access to justice · 2023

kps.k: The main proposed mechanism is to relieve delivery burdens while preserving human legal work and relationships.
kps.d: Natalie Anne Knowlton proposes first drafts of public legal information, procedural guidance, intake and triage. Sateesh Nori adds translation, court forms and preventive information, arguing that less operational friction could free lawyers to address why clients face legal problems. These are proposed uses, not established task-performance findings. Amanda Brown argues that technology should facilitate human interaction rather than take it over, while Oborn frames AI as staff support rather than wholesale job replacement. Alongside this augmentation model, Moon predicts that people will use AI independently whether professionals assist them or not; that prediction does not establish safe or effective self-help.

qs.q: So think about content generation, providing first drafts of content generation for external facing audiences with respect to legal information and how to navigate the flow of a process.
qs.a: AI's Potential for Access to Justice · Access to justice · 2023

qs.q: And for the first time in my career, I’m seeing a path forward out of the kind of mess of intake and triage that we’re all stuck in a way forward that allows us to do that type of work that only we can do.
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: Reported uptake and concrete projects show activity, but most excerpts do not demonstrate improved access or legal outcomes.
kps.d: Moon attributes a twofold AI-adoption rate among legal-aid professionals relative to other lawyers to the 2025 report How Technology Can Help Bridge the Justice Gap; the excerpts omit definitions, sampling and explanations for the difference. She also gives a qualitative account of researchers providing roughly 100 legal-aid participants with paid ChatGPT access, highlighting those who received learning support. Separately, the Chien–Kim discussion identifies a field study and a resource containing 100 use cases without supplying methods or results. Lone Star Legal Aid’s grant-supported three-chatbot project and Nori’s tenant repair-rights tool provide implementation examples, not measured evidence that they reduced unmet need.

qs.q: Apparently legal aid professionals are embracing AI at twice the rate of other lawyers and other results are promising as well.
qs.a: Why Is Legal Aid Embracing AI Faster than Other Legal Professionals? — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: They put in the hands of people, about a hundred people, access to the paid versions of chat GPT, and just let people go to see what they could do, what they could build, and the results were pretty extraordinary.
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: Thomson Reuters’ AI for Justice program supplies specific reported gains, while leaving their generalisability and system-wide significance unresolved.
kps.d: The 2025 LawNext introduction reports attorneys saving up to 15 hours weekly, organisations serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials prepared up to 75% faster. These are upper-bound claims, not averages. The introduction links them to quicker protection orders, tenants returning home sooner and earlier exoneration filings, but the supplied material gives no measurement methodology or basis for assessing attribution and representativeness. The episode itself asks whether such gains can substantially close the justice gap rather than make marginal progress against a growing problem.

qs.q: The results have been significant: attorneys are saving up to 15 hours per week, organizations are serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials are being prepared up to 75% faster.
qs.a: How AI Is Helping Legal Aid Serve 50% More Clients — Thomson Reuters AI for Justice Program One Year In · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: But more importantly, these efficiency gains are translating into real-world impact  – domestic violence victims receiving protection orders more quickly, wrongfully evicted tenants getting back into their homes before their possessions are destroyed, and innocent people in prison having their exoneration petitions filed years sooner.
qs.a: How AI Is Helping Legal Aid Serve 50% More Clients — Thomson Reuters AI for Justice Program One Year In · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: The central tension concerns how urgently to deploy AI and what evidence should justify reliance.
kps.d: An unidentified opening speaker in the Hagan–Nori discussion argues that the justice crisis demands using tools available now rather than dwelling on potential harms. In contrast, Jason Tashea questions present deployment justified by promises of future improvement. These are contrasting emphases across discussions, not a direct exchange. Angela Tripp proposes task-specific comparisons with human error rates as a way to reassure sceptics, but supplies no evidence that AI meets that standard. Knowlton’s expectation of better privacy controls likewise remains tentative. Together, the excerpts distinguish urgency and optimism from demonstrated reliability, without specifying a common deployment threshold.

qs.q: We can navel gaze and think about the bad potential outcomes all day long, but this is a crisis.
qs.a: Margaret Hagan & Sateesh Nori — putting AI to the test for legal services: lab-to-pilot pipelines and the crisis case for urgency · Access to justice · 2024

qs.q: Today I’m told AI is going to be different, but it often feels like a technology wanting to be implemented today that promises to be better tomorrow.
qs.a: Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

kps.k: The practical agenda extends beyond software access to community-led design, training, procurement and sustained institutional support.
kps.d: Moon recommends understanding community needs before building solutions; Kim advocates training and shared learning. Thomson Reuters combines CoCounsel access with nonprofit-specific support, while LSC grants, peer-learning resources and shared guidance offer infrastructure for experimentation. Procurement work with pro bono counsel aims to help legal-aid leaders identify AI-specific purchasing issues. Oborn advises allowing an extra six months for implementation. These recommendations address the difficulty of reaching fragmented, resource-constrained organisations, but the excerpts do not establish which support model works best. The resulting agenda is purposeful, supported experimentation aimed at client benefit—not adoption as an end in itself.

qs.q: You did some human-centered research first to figure out what the needs were in the community you’re serving.
qs.a: Talking AI for Access to Justice at the 25th Innovations in Technology Conference — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: And I really want to encourage the broader legal community to be thinking that way and to be putting on trainings to enable the next generation to also learn as they’re coming into the legal practice and just all work together to share our learnings to increase access to justice.
qs.a: Colleen Chien, Miriam Kim & Breon Austin — the generative-AI-and-legal-aid field study, discussed with a participating clinic · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: These curated sources from regulators, courts and professional bodies do not provide enough substantive evidence to establish a collective position on the proposition that AI can expand capacity for unmet civil legal need while preserving human relationships, but that demonstrated access gains remain limited. Their common emphasis is preparatory: helping lawyers and judges understand fast-moving AI developments and insisting that innovation serve a purposeful institutional objective. This is compatible with the cluster’s agenda of supported, deliberate experimentation, but it neither endorses the proposed access-to-justice mechanisms nor evaluates their results, risks or effects on human legal work. There is material internal variation in proximity to the proposition: Kellye Testy’s rejection of disruption for its own sake aligns normatively with purposeful adoption, and the programme framing connects technology with expanding access to justice; Jen Leonard’s excerpts are more narrowly educational, concentrating on AI literacy and translating technological developments for legal professionals. None of the supplied excerpts addresses legal-aid capacity, task-specific reliability, measured client outcomes or preservation of lawyer-client relationships directly, so support should not be inferred from thematic compatibility alone.

qs.q: # How Law Schools Are Embracing Flexibility, Justice and AI — full episode transcript  *Kellye Testy — Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network (2026)*  Kellye Testy:  We don’t have to choose between excellence and innovation.
qs.a: How Law Schools Are Embracing Flexibility, Justice and AI — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2026

qs.q: On every episode, we try our best to keep up with the rapid pace of change in the land of AI and draw connections for lawyers who are practicing all day, judges who are overseeing their dockets and may not have time to keep pace with AI developments, and think about what those developments mean in the legal profession.
qs.a: Generative AI and the Courts: Expanding Legal Access or Opening the Floodgates? — full episode transcript · Regulators & courts · 2025

vlens.an: The academia-and-research sources support the proposition’s agenda of purposeful, supported experimentation rather than treating AI adoption itself as proof of access-to-justice gains. Their common rationale is that preparation, investigation and professional learning should begin before wider legal deployment, while AI’s potential to equalise access must be pursued deliberately rather than assumed. Both remain consistent with the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: the supplied excerpts provide recommendations, research activity and use-case resources, but no methods or measured improvements in access or legal outcomes. There is material variation in emphasis: the legal-ethics discussion focuses broadly on individual readiness and introductory learning, whereas the legal-aid field-study discussion ties deliberate research, training and shared learning directly to increasing access to justice. These curated sources indicate alignment within the supplied academic and research voice, not the prevalence of that view across academia generally.

qs.q: In the meantime, I hope that those who work in those kinds of settings will at least on their own, discover the potential so that when the time comes to roll it out in a law related setting, they’re ready.
qs.a: Do Existing Legal Ethics Rules Cover AI? — full episode transcript · Academia · 2024

vlens.an: This curated access-to-justice and civil-society voice supports the proposition that AI should be used primarily to expand capacity for unmet civil legal need while preserving human legal work and requiring evidence before reliance. Common reasons include relieving intake, triage, drafting, translation and form-preparation burdens; helping legal-aid and pro bono providers serve more people; and enabling lawyers to focus on clients’ underlying problems and human relationships. The sources generally distinguish implementation activity, adoption and optimistic predictions from demonstrated access or legal outcomes. Material internal variation concerns pace and mode of deployment: some urge immediate experimentation because the justice gap is already a crisis, while others warn against deploying systems on promises of future improvement and call for task-specific reliability evidence, community-led design, training, procurement guidance and implementation support. Most favour augmentation, although Moon also predicts unavoidable self-directed public use, which raises a separate question about safe self-help. The Thomson Reuters account reports specific upper-bound capacity and speed gains, but leaves methodology, generalisability and system-wide effects unresolved. One introductory source is unclear because it identifies advocates and their credentials without supplying their arguments. These selected sources should not be treated as representative of all access-to-justice or civil-society professionals.

qs.q: — full episode transcript  *Amanda Brown — Talk Justice, Legal Services Corporation / Legal Talk Network (2025)*  Amanda Brown:  This is a human endeavor that we’re on, and we should just be using technology as a tool to facilitate those interactions instead of offloading them.
qs.a: What Is Human-Centered Legal Help in the Age of AI? — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: The results have been significant: attorneys are saving up to 15 hours per week, organizations are serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials are being prepared up to 75% faster.
qs.a: How AI Is Helping Legal Aid Serve 50% More Clients — Thomson Reuters AI for Justice Program One Year In · Access to justice · 2025

elens.an: The curated 2023–2024 sources support the proposition’s central framing of generative AI as a potential capacity-expander for unmet civil legal need, while consistently distinguishing experimentation from proven access gains. Common reasons include the scale of the justice gap, opportunities to reduce provider-side burdens through drafting, intake and triage, the prospect of scaling pro bono and self-help, and the need for training, shared resources and institutional preparation. Most claims are recommendations, proposed use cases, project descriptions or predictions rather than measured findings about improved access or legal outcomes. Material variation concerns pace and mode of adoption: some speakers urge immediate use because the justice gap is a crisis, whereas others emphasise deliberate investigation, safety, privacy, collaboration and groundwork before deployment. The augmentation model is clearest where technology supports volunteer attorneys or legal-service providers, although one source predicts independent public use regardless of professional involvement. One general AI-literacy source does not address access to justice closely enough to establish a position. Overall, these sources align with purposeful experimentation for client benefit but provide little evidence that activity had yet produced reliable, generalisable access gains.

qs.q: And so I thought we need to talk about this and how legal aid organizations and folks who are interested in bringing these tools to bear to serve more people, help them solve their legal problems, should be approaching these tools, things to think about, actual things we can do right now, concerns and maybe some heed and care we should take with these tools.
qs.a: AI's Potential for Access to Justice · Access to justice · 2023

elens.an: The curated 2025 sources support the proposition that AI can augment legal-aid capacity, but that adoption and implementation activity exceed well-established access-to-justice outcomes. Common reasons include the prospect of relieving intake, triage, translation, forms and other delivery burdens; preserving lawyers’ attention for complex human and systemic questions; and combining software with training, community-led design, procurement guidance and institutional support. Material variation concerns confidence and evidentiary strength: Thomson Reuters’ AI for Justice account reports substantial upper-bound capacity and speed gains linked to client benefits, while other sources offer practitioner expectations, qualitative experimentation or implementation examples without measured outcomes. Some emphasise task-specific reliability evidence and warn against deploying systems on promises of future improvement; others stress urgency and optimism. Human-centred sources specifically insist that technology facilitate rather than replace legal relationships. Two introductory excerpts provide too little substantive material to determine alignment, but they do not contradict the proposition. Overall, these selected sources favour purposeful augmentation while leaving generalisability, reliability thresholds and system-wide effects on the justice gap unresolved.

qs.q: The results have been significant: attorneys are saving up to 15 hours per week, organizations are serving as many as 50% more clients daily, and urgent case materials are being prepared up to 75% faster.
qs.a: How AI Is Helping Legal Aid Serve 50% More Clients — Thomson Reuters AI for Justice Program One Year In · Access to justice · 2025

qs.q: Today I’m told AI is going to be different, but it often feels like a technology wanting to be implemented today that promises to be better tomorrow.
qs.a: Preventing Harm Amidst the AI Hype — full episode transcript · Access to justice · 2025

elens.an: The 2026 sources support the proposition’s central, qualified case for justice augmentation: technology—and, in the Lone Star source, AI specifically—is framed as a way to expand legal-aid capacity and access while assisting staff rather than replacing human legal work. They also reinforce the proposition’s institutional agenda through grant funding, sector-wide participation and purposeful implementation. Material variation concerns specificity and evidentiary strength. Lone Star provides the clearest AI implementation example through its three-chatbot project, but describes expected scaling and impact rather than measured improvements in access or legal outcomes, and notes that deployment takes longer than anticipated. LSC’s technology-report discussion supports responsive funding and collective action but addresses justice technology broadly and supplies no effectiveness evidence. Testy’s remarks are compatible with deliberate, client-benefiting experimentation because they reject disruption for its own sake, yet they do not establish a position on AI-driven legal-aid capacity or preservation of human relationships. Overall, the period’s evidence endorses the proposition’s direction while exemplifying its warning that implementation activity and aspiration exceed demonstrated access gains. These curated sources should not be treated as representative of all 2026 views.

qs.q: Well, I’m a big believer in the potential of technology and specifically artificial intelligence to help us expand access to justice by scaling in a lot of ways.
